visible.summary:
Iraq is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it now has one of the world's most explicitly anti-trans statutes, in force since 1 July 2024. Amendments to the 1988 anti-prostitution law criminalise same-sex relationships (10–15 years), “biological sex change based on personal desire and inclination” (criminalising transition itself), and men who “intentionally act like women” (1–3 years) — a direct statutory criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Promoting homosexuality carries a minimum 7-year sentence. President Rashid signed the law on 29 June 2024.

Behind the statute stands a documented milieu of lethal violence: militia-led campaigns against men perceived as gay or gender-nonconforming (HRW's “They Want Us Exterminated” documented mutilated bodies dumped as warnings), with impunity. Most LGBT Iraqis hide their identity entirely. The Kurdistan Region has not passed the federal law but shares the social climate and has no protections.

For a visitor: being visibly trans is a statutory offence; discovery risks 1–3 years, with severe custodial and militia risk beyond the legal penalty.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex relationships criminalised at 10–15 years under the 2024 amendments — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The 1988-law amendments apply in federal Iraq; the suspended KRI parliament has not adopted them, but no protection exists there either.

sources.claim: HRW (20 May 2024): Iraq's parliament passed (27 Apr 2024) an anti-LGBT amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution — same-sex relations punishable by 10-15 years' prison, 1-3 years for undergoing/performing gender-affirming procedures; HRW calls for repeal.

BBC: the new law criminalises same-sex relationships with 10-15 years' jail, 1-3 years for transgender people, plus penalties for 'promoting homosexuality' — framed by supporters as upholding religious values, condemned by rights groups.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry (May 2024) documents Iraq's new law prohibiting prostitution, homosexuality and gender-change procedures.

ILGA Asia briefing (15 Jan 2025): on 28 Apr 2024 Iraq amended the 1988 prostitution law to explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression; signed by the President 29 Jun 2024 — the operative legal baseline.

UK Home Office CPIN Iraq: Sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v3.0, July 2025): assessment of risk from state and hybrid actors and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Iraq: documents sectarian violence, torture, impunity, and 'societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity' - official acknowledgment of the dangers facing LGBT Iraqis.
CNN (27 Oct 2023): prominent Iraqi TikToker fatally shot in Baghdad amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community — targeted killing of a visible figure as the anti-LGBT climate hardened.

BBC investigation: dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people killed in recent years in post-occupation Iraq while authorities turn a blind eye — the UN says state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator; documented culture of abuse and impunity for anti-LGBT violence.

visible.summary:
Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care.

Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.
visible.tangentialFactors: Marriage equality since 2020 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: The administrative name/photo ID process (which does not change the sex marker) and universal healthcare covering transition-related care are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: ID sex-marker limits and Church influence are resident-facing/climate.

sources.claim: Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex conduct legal since 1971; first Central American country to adopt marriage equality (2020); since 2018 (Executive Decree 41173-MP) legal gender change on documents without surgery or court order; state health system funds gender-affirming care; rollback pressure — conversion-therapy bill stalled since its 2019 committee report, and in 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education program and the 2022 anti-LGBT-bullying protocol.
ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Costa Rica: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, gender recognition and protections.

UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, report on her July 2023 visit to Costa Rica (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

GayLawNet Costa Rica legal reference: survivor's pension extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (Ministry of Labor announcement 25 Jun 2016; individual survivor benefit approved 29 Jun 2018; teachers' separate budget excluded); also records the 2000 Supreme Court ruling that IVF is unconstitutional — dated partnership-benefits context.

PinkNews (1 May 2008): the Costa Rican government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia (17 May); President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate, promote and support activities 'directed at the eradication of homophobia' — credit to LGBT group CIPAC.

The Tico Times (16 May 2014): President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May (officially recognised since 2008); lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties called it a 'provocation' while a same-sex civil union bill was pending — organised political opposition alongside official recognition.

visible.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below Northern Triangle levels.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2008 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2023 marriage ruling is a climate signal.
visible.localsOnly: The surgery-required LGR process is resident-facing; the documented employment exclusion affects residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Surgery requirement for LGR and marriage ruling are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Outright International current Panama overview: amendment of the general anti-discrimination law to include SOGI grounds was blocked by the National Assembly in 2024 (claiming implicit coverage), no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited; at the 2025 UN UPR multiple states urged explicit anti-discrimination protections, gender-recognition reform and stronger violence safeguards — legal reforms remain stalled and Panama lags much of Latin America.

Equaldex data for Panama: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment/housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked #18 of 22).

Washington Blade (16 Feb 2018): Supreme Court Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega withdrew his October 2017 draft ruling against marriage rights — the draft had held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while suggesting the Assembly consider civil unions; the Panama government signalled it would comply with the landmark 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision.

BBC features (14 Aug 2018): in Panama's Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing 'third gender' community (Omeggid) is accepted as completely normal, with powerful matriarchal figures elevating women's status — cultural context for how gender diversity is received in this part of the country.

Outright International current Panama overview (fetched page resolves to the country overview): anti-discrimination amendment blocked by the National Assembly in 2024, no hate-crime recognition, unregulated intersex infant surgery, 2025 UPR calls for SOGI protections and gender-recognition reform, reforms stalled.

Washington Blade (22 Oct 2017): La Estrella reported Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega's draft ruling finding the family-code sections barring same-sex marriage 'not unconstitutional' while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions ('equality must be constitutionally guaranteed via the law'); the two marriage lawsuits (a UK-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge) were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition.

visible.summary:
Albania is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; a National LGBTI Action Plan (2021–2027) is in force (implementation is admittedly flawed); and the UN Independent Expert on SOGI conducted a full country visit in July 2024 — a sign of government openness unusual for the region. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, no bathroom laws, no documented police targeting; the realistic risk is social hostility outside Tirana and along more conservative rural areas. EU candidate status is driving slow alignment.
visible.tangentialFactors: No SOGI hate-crime statute, and discrimination in key areas drew European Parliament concern — relevant mainly to visitors who experience or witness bias incidents.
visible.localsOnly: There is no legal gender recognition (Albania rejected a self-ID recommendation at its UPR) — a resident-facing gap that does not affect a foreign passport holder.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and action-plan implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: End-of-mission statement of the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity after the country visit to Albania, 1-12 July 2024: assesses good practices and challenges and offers recommendations to the State — the international-review baseline for Albanian SOGI conditions.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) Albania chapter: discrimination complaints filed over the film 'Strange World' screenings were mediated, with the Commissioner ruling in favour in one case; Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people; groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

UN report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 (17 Jun 2025) by Independent Expert Graeme Reid on the Albania visit of 1-12 Jul 2024: evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.

PinkNews (Feb 5, 2010): Albania passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation but without same-sex marriage; homosexuality had carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for gay marriage in July 2009, framing the law as EU-integration driven.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda' — a record of parliamentary hostility toward LGBT education work under the Berisha-led opposition.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): MP Nard Ndoka's Facebook post branding the government 'LGBT' and accusing it of pushing LGBT values in schools, illustrating political anti-LGBT messaging in the same week as the schools campaign row.

Balkan Insight (Oct 27, 2011): Albania's Anti-Discrimination Commissioner reprimanded ruling Democratic Party MP Tritian Shehu for telling parliament that 'homosexuality is a disease and should be treated with hormones', warning him to avoid remarks that create an atmosphere of tension toward the LGBT community.

visible.summary:
Montenegro is workable for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.
visible.tangentialFactors: The 2020 same-sex partnership law — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
visible.localsOnly: No LGR law (administrative practice inconsistent) — resident-facing; the misdemeanour-overuse practice affects resident victims.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: LGR inconsistency and prosecution-practice gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.

Human Dignity Trust global legal history (updated 18 June 2026): Montenegro appears among the 1977 European decriminalisations (Croatia/Slovenia/Montenegro cohort); reference source for MNE's decriminalisation date rather than MNE-specific analysis.

GlobalGayz (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. Dated but concrete on social climate.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

visible.summary:
Uzbekistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — and Human Dignity Trust notes transgender people may be targeted under it, since there is no legal gender recognition and trans people are legally their birth sex. There is substantial evidence of recent enforcement: frequent arrests, and extortion by threat of arrest, with police as the most common perpetrators of anti-LGBT violence; torture goes unpunished (HRW). Because of criminalisation, victims cannot report violence to authorities.

ECOM's 2024 national report documents continuing rights violations, and the Justice Ministry denies registration to independent human-rights groups — no community infrastructure can operate openly. There is no documented trans-visitor case, but the legal mechanism (birth-sex status + Art 120) means a trans visitor discovered in a same-sex-appearing relationship faces direct prosecution risk, and discovery itself invites extortion.
visible.tangentialFactors: Article 120 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; extortion-by-threat-of-arrest targets discovered trans people.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Art 120 formally applies to male same-sex conduct; its application to trans people is via birth-sex legal status — a direct mechanism, not merely climate.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Uzbekistan's criminalisation of same-sex activity (Article 120 of the criminal code, up to 3 years).

HRW World Report 2024 (events of 2023): same-sex conduct between men remains criminalised (up to 3 years); police target gay/bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment; forced 'forced examinations' amount to torture per WHO; impunity for police ill-treatment persists.

ECOM national report (2024) on violations of the rights of LGBT people in Uzbekistan: legislation, anti-discrimination legislation, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, right to health and right to work.

UK Home Office COI note (Jul 2024): consensual same-sex conduct between men criminalised under Article 120 of the 1994 Criminal Code, up to 3 years; documented Article 120 cases 2009-2023; police intimidation/violence/exploitation of gay men and trans people routine; LGBTI orgs cannot register, operate unofficially; rural taboo drives discrimination.

US State Dept 2021 HRR: Section 6 documents legal and societal abuses -- torture/ill-treatment and arbitrary detention concerns in custody, plus social stigma and violence affecting LGBT people under the criminalised framework.

US State Dept 2023 HRR: LGBTQI+ people arrested then released or threatened with arrest unless paying bribes; police coerced LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison; websites and bloggers self-censored on LGBTQI+ issues; societal harassment continued.

HRW (23 Mar 2021): Article 120 punishes consensual sex between males up to 3 years; gay/bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from state and non-state actors with almost no protections; HRW urges decriminalisation (Uzbekistan then on UN rights council).
